lesson.title: The Noise Floor: Audio's Absolute Silence Isn't Silent
lesson.summary: The noise floor is the total residual noise level present in a system with no signal applied, combining thermal noise with every other noise source, and it defines the quietest level at which a signal can still be meaningfully distinguished.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter looked at thermal noise from a single resistor in isolation. A real circuit, though, is full of resistors, transistors, and wiring, and every one of them contributes some noise. Add up all of those contributions, thermal noise from resistances, shot noise and flicker noise from semiconductors, hum picked up from power supplies, interference coupled into wiring, and you get the noise floor: the residual signal level a system produces even when nothing useful is being fed into it. Thermal noise, from the last chapter, is usually the fundamental, unavoidable part of that floor, but in a real piece of gear it is rarely the only contributor.

The noise floor matters because it sets a hard limit on what a circuit can usefully do. Any signal that arrives below the noise floor at a given point in a circuit is not just quiet, it is gone, mixed inextricably with random noise, and no amount of amplification later in the signal chain can pull it back out. Amplifying after the point where noise was added just makes the signal and the noise louder together, in the same ratio. This is why the design of the very first, most sensitive stage in a circuit matters so much: whatever noise floor gets established there effectively becomes the noise floor for everything downstream.

Here is a worked example connecting back to the previous chapter and forward to the dBu chapter. Recall the 10 kΩ resistor's thermal noise over a 20 kHz bandwidth: 1.79 microvolts RMS. Express that noise floor in dBu, using the 0.775 V reference: dBu = 20 times log10(1.79 times 10 to the negative 6 divided by 0.775). The ratio inside the log is 1.79 times 10 to the negative 6 divided by 0.775, which equals 2.310 times 10 to the negative 6. The base ten log of that is about negative 5.636. Multiplying by 20 gives about negative 112.7. So this resistor's thermal noise floor sits at roughly negative 112.7 dBu, a genuinely tiny level relative to typical operating signals.

Real circuits generally show a somewhat higher noise floor than this pure resistor calculation, since it ignores the semiconductor noise and other sources mentioned above, but the thermal noise calculation sets the best case floor a real design can ever hope to approach. This is exactly why preamp datasheets often specify an equivalent input noise figure in dBu or dBV, using the fixed reference voltage tools from the previous chapter to describe how close a real design gets to that theoretical thermal limit. With a defined noise floor in hand, the next chapter puts a wanted signal on top of it and asks how far above that floor the signal actually sits.
